messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The intersection had been dark and slick with November rain. Arthur Vance remembered the sudden, violent intrusion of another vehicle’s headlights, the sickening crack of reinforced glass, and the immediate, breathless certainty that he would not walk away. The T-bone collision folded his sedan’s passenger side inward, pinning him against the wheel just long enough for the airbag to detonate. When he finally clawed onto the wet asphalt, the engine died, leaving only the hiss of the radiator and distant sirens. That night, his world collapsed into a single sequence of metal and motion. In the months that followed, Arthur returned to his interior design practice, but the studio no longer felt safe. While reviewing hardwood samples with a contractor at a client’s kitchen, a delivery van reversed abruptly and backfired with a sharp crack. Arthur froze, his pen hovering over the invoice. The sound instantly pulled a fragmented image of the other driver’s door into his mind, the metal twisted inward, vivid and unbidden. He began tracing the outline of crumpled bumpers on his drafting paper, describing the exact angle of the shattered windshield to anyone who asked. Within days, the sound of any engine starting nearby sent a jolt through his chest, and he found himself checking traffic reports while waiting for drivers. He also began to flinch when clients mentioned a recent highway pile-up, his attention fracturing every time the conversation drifted toward wrecked vehicles or collision mechanics. He stopped taking side streets, taking long routes around the city to keep the hum of traffic at a distance. Alongside the external alarms, Arthur’s internal landscape had shifted. When he stood before the mirror in his changing room, he could no longer recognize the man staring back. The deliberate posture of his former self, the quiet confidence he had once brought to every client meeting, felt foreign. He caught himself apologizing for minor stumbles, as though his limbs had forgotten how to cooperate with his intentions. He had come to believe he could no longer trust his own body to steady him without warning. The quiet reassurance he once felt when climbing scaffolding was gone, replaced by a constant calculation of how much strain his joints could bear. What remained was the unshakable sense that he had permanently changed for the worse. The loss of his former identity sat beside the conviction that the alteration was irreversible, two parallel realities he carried through every workday. Now, at fifty-seven, Arthur scheduled an intake after a recent site visit left him unable to return to his desk. He had been measuring window trim when a car alarm triggered outside, and the sudden cascade of bleeps sent him to the floor, knees buckling. He sat on the subfloor for twenty minutes, waiting for the sensation to pass, certain that if he pushed through it, his body would simply fail him. He is seeking help not to erase the accident, but to stop living in the waiting room of his own nervous system. He hopes to reclaim the ability to walk down a city street without bracing for impact, and to sit in his studio without the constant fear that the man who once designed spaces no longer knows how to inhabit his own.
